CX language reference (development edition) ​

This is the concise reference for the language currently implemented by cxc. The compiler and runtime are in active development; unsupported syntax is rejected and this document is not a promise of source or binary compatibility. The checked-in ANTLR grammars are the detailed syntax source. Runtime ownership rules are in standard-library-contracts.md.

Source files and names ​

A source file contains optional import directives, an optional namespace declaration, and declarations. Namespaces and imports qualify type and function names. Identifiers use ASCII letters or _ initially, followed by ASCII letters, digits, or _. Whitespace, // line comments, and /* ... */ comments are ignored.

Integer literals support decimal, octal (0...), hexadecimal (0x...), and binary (0b...) forms with optional u and l suffixes. Floating literals use a decimal point and optional exponent, with optional f, d, or m suffix. Character and string literals accept the escapes \\, \', \", \n, \r, \t, \b, and \0. String storage and character behavior are described in the runtime contracts.

Types and declarations ​

Built-in scalar types are bool, char, signed sbyte, short, int, long, unsigned byte, ushort, uint, ulong, float, and double. string and object are reference types; ptr is an opaque pointer. void is a return type. Types can be nullable with ? and arrays with []. CX also supports enums, structs, classes, interfaces, properties, constructors, generic declarations, and generic methods. Generic implementations are specialized for closed types; only the supported generic body and layout patterns described by compiler diagnostics are accepted.

Fixed-width numeric spellings are aliases for the existing built-in types:

AliasBuilt-in type
int8sbyte
int16short
int32int
int64long
uint8byte
uint16ushort
uint32uint
uint64ulong
float32float
float64double

These spellings have identical type identity, conversions, reflection metadata, and generated C representation, including inside arrays, delegates, and typed pointers. They do not introduce distinct types or overloads. Native C integer types whose widths vary by platform use the separate System.Interop scalar aliases described in the native interop section.

Classes support single class inheritance and multiple interfaces. Interfaces can inherit multiple interfaces. Members can be public, protected, private, or internal. Methods support static, virtual, abstract, override, and final; const methods/accessors promise not to mutate the receiver through that member. Properties and indexers use get and set accessors. Accessors without bodies on class or struct properties synthesize private backing storage. Structs and classes use constructors; constructor initializers can call this(...) or base(...). A class with no declared constructor receives an implicit parameterless constructor. Declaring any constructor suppresses that implicit constructor. An implicit derived-class constructor calls the base class's parameterless constructor.

Classes inherit Object.ToString(), which returns the runtime type name as a string. This method is available on class instances and uses runtime type metadata, including for derived classes.

Object.Equals(object) compares reference identity by default, and GetHashCode() returns a hash derived from that identity, so the hash stays consistent for the same object while it remains alive. All three object methods are virtual and can be overridden to provide value-based equality and a matching hash implementation. String overrides them: ToString() returns the string, Equals(object) compares string contents, and GetHashCode() hashes the UTF-8 contents. String == and != also compare contents using ordinal, case-sensitive comparison.

Locals may state their type or use var with an initializer. Local functions are available inside blocks. They can call each other and recurse. A local function can capture a preceding local variable or parameter by reference, so later assignments are visible to the local function. Generic local functions can infer type arguments from a call and use the supported generic function body patterns and type constraints in generics-design.md. They may also declare exact closed specializations in the same block as the primary local function. The specialization inherits the primary's constraints, can capture the same enclosing locals, and is selected after ordinary local function overload resolution; other closed type arguments use the primary body. Generic functions and methods may also define a closed replacement by listing closed type arguments after the function name, for example public int Adjust&lt;int&gt;(int value) { return value + 1; }. The compiler classifies declaration lists after visible types and imports are collected: unresolved simple identifiers introduce generic parameters, while a visible type name or any non-identifier type form makes the list a specialization. Specialization lists must provide the primary's full generic arity and use closed type arguments; partial lists and arguments that depend on an open containing type are rejected. Specializations inherit default parameter values from the primary and cannot declare different defaults. Calls that select the matching generic declaration use that body after checking the primary declaration's constraints; other closed type arguments use the primary body. The signature must match after substitution. This slice currently applies to top-level functions and static or instance methods on non-generic classes and structs. Public specializations on these targets can be consumed through project references and are emitted by their defining project. Method-level generic methods may be declared virtual, override, or abstract. Closed calls from non-generic callers dispatch through a typed runtime registration keyed by the receiver's runtime class and the closed method type arguments. Virtual and override specializations replace the selected implementation for exact type arguments; otherwise that override's primary body runs. Generic virtual methods and overrides on generic reference classes also dispatch this way when the containing owner is closed at the call site. Generic interface methods, including constructed generic interfaces, dispatch through ordinary and supported closed generic class implementations. Class virtual methods and overrides also support a class constraint combined with three interfaces, and a struct constraint combined with three interfaces, including consumer overrides across project references. Generic callers support the documented direct forwarding call, matching local-result, and void-call shapes, including conditional if/if-else returns with block-wrapped branches and leading explicit bool or inferred var locals initialized by supported boolean expressions controlling dispatch, when method arguments and receiver types close for each caller specialization. The consuming project registers known implementations of referenced generic interfaces, including exact specializations under static and DLL linking. In statement-level forwarding returns, explicitly typed copies of the caller's return type parameter may form a chain from a matching parameter; the copies may use an explicit type or var, may appear before or after leading boolean locals, and may supply both the virtual-call argument and fallback return. In interface inheritance, a generic method redeclared with the same signature on both branches of a diamond shares one dispatch target and supports exact specialization and primary-body fallback. Other generic caller body shapes, unsupported closed class layouts or overrides, and runtime-loaded types outside the compiled project graph remain unsupported. Generic specializations of abstract methods cannot provide an implementation. A consumer may declare a project-local replacement for an imported public top-level generic function in the same namespace. It affects calls and delegate bindings in that consumer only, takes precedence over the library's matching specialization, and falls back to the primary body for unmatched type arguments. See generic-dependency-specializations-design.md. The virtual-dispatch constraint and acceptance matrix are recorded in generic-virtual-specializations-design.md. A primary generic function or method on a non-static, non-generic class or struct may also return one inferred generic call that forwards one or more direct parameters whose types are matching caller type parameters to a generic function or method, either directly or through one explicitly typed or inferred matching local that is returned; the target resolves separately for each closed caller instance. Instance-method forwarding supports the current receiver of the same non-generic class or struct, a class receiver expression whose resolved type exactly matches the target method's non-generic owner, or a struct receiver expression whose type exactly matches its owner. Class expressions are evaluated once; struct lvalues retain their location and struct rvalues are copied to one temporary. Forwarded arguments may include pure built-in expressions over literals and concrete parameters, as long as a direct generic parameter argument is also present. Calls, assignments, increments, overloaded operators and other open-body forms remain unsupported. Binding a generic function or a supported static/instance generic method to a delegate uses the expected signature to close it and selects the matching custom implementation or primary body. Generic virtual forwarding calls are also supported in generic methods declared on a generic class when the owner is closed at each call site. The owner type arguments are substituted while resolving the virtual method arguments; exact specialization and primary-body fallback are available through class and interface contracts. Other generic caller body shapes and open owner contexts remain unsupported. Static generic methods on generic classes can be called through a closed owner, for example Utility&lt;string&gt;.Select&lt;int&gt;(value). The owner type arguments are checked against the class constraints and close the method signature before ordinary overload resolution and specialization selection. Static calls do not construct an instance of the owner type. Instance fields are initialized to zero unless assigned by a constructor. Static fields can have expressions initialized during module startup, after referenced modules initialize. A class or struct may declare one static constructor(). It cannot have an access modifier, parameters, or a constructor initializer. Static field initializers run before static constructors; static constructors then run once in generated type declaration order and before the executable entry point. A static constructor does not suppress an implicit instance parameterless constructor.

Compatible partial class, struct, and interface declarations merge their members into one type. The declarations must agree on kind, generic parameters, visibility, and type modifiers. Base types from each declaration are combined; the normal inheritance rules still reject conflicting class bases or duplicate interfaces.

alias Alias = ExistingName; declares a transparent alias for a named type. The target may include type arguments, as in alias IntBox = Box&lt;int&gt;;. An alias may also declare generic parameters and substitute them in its target, as in alias BoxOf&lt;T&gt; = Box&lt;T&gt;;. Aliases may refer to types declared later, in another source file, or through another alias. They do not create a distinct runtime type. Alias targets must resolve to named types.

An extension declaration adds instance methods and properties to a class, struct, interface, or enum. Generic targets use the target's type parameters in the same order, for example public extension BoxExtensions&lt;T&gt; : Box&lt;T&gt;. Concrete array types such as int[] may also be targets for ordinary extension methods. Generic element patterns such as T[], T[][], and Box&lt;T&gt;[] may target extension methods and close their generic arguments from the receiver. Array extension properties on concrete and generic array targets must be read-only, and their property type and accessor parameters must be concrete and independent of the element type. Concrete and generic array targets support non-mutating unary and binary extension operators. Concrete and generic array targets may define +=, -=, *=, /=, or %= when the operator parameter and return type match the array target; generic operators close from the receiver type. The returned array reference is assigned back to the left operand. Array ++ and -- operators may also return the matching array target type; postfix forms preserve the old reference while writing back the returned one. Public extensions can target public types from referenced projects and are available to consumers that import the extension's namespace:

cx
import Types;
namespace Extensions;

public extension FooExtensions : Foo {
    public int DoubledValue { const get => Value * 2; }
    public void Invert() { Value = -Value; }
}

The compiler emits extension methods and property accessors in the declaring module, with the target value passed as the receiver. Primitive and enum targets support instance methods and read-only properties with value receivers; their extension operators support non-mutating unary and binary forms. Primitive and enum extension ++, --, and compound assignment operators take and return values; the compiler writes the result back to the assignable operand. Postfix increment and decrement preserve the previous operand value. For an interface target, the interface value is passed directly and calls inside the extension preserve interface dispatch. Member lookup remains a compile-time operation; no runtime extension wrapper is created. Extensions cannot declare fields or constructors; target parameters substitute through method signatures, and method-level generic functions can be inferred and specialized by consuming projects, subject to the existing generic body restrictions. An extension may declare an operator for a class, struct, interface, or enum target; the operator is considered only when the extension's namespace is imported, and lookup uses the left operand's type with exact parameter matching.

Generic extension methods on class, struct, interface, enum, primitive, and concrete or generic array targets may declare exact closed method specializations using the same keyword-free form as other generic methods. The compiler selects a matching specialization after resolving the primary method and checking its constraints; unmatched type arguments use the primary body. This is supported for ordinary and constructed generic class targets, struct targets, interface targets including constructed generic interfaces, enum targets, primitive targets, and concrete or generic array targets. Generic binary operator methods may also declare closed specializations. The compiler infers their method arguments from the operands, checks the primary constraints, and selects a matching custom body; other type arguments use the primary operator body. This includes generic mutating +=, -=, *=, /=, and %= methods: a matching specialization can mutate the struct receiver, while an unmatched operand uses the constrained primary body. Generic non-mutating unary operator methods infer their method arguments from the expected result type, since they have no explicit operands. The result type must determine every method type argument. The primary constraints are checked before specialization selection; unmatched closed arguments use the primary body. Mutating ++ and -- do not infer method arguments from a result context.

Expressions, conversions, and overloads ​

Expressions include member access, calls, indexing, object and array creation, unary and binary operators, assignment and compound assignment, conditional expressions, ??, is, and explicit as casts. &&, ||, ??, and the conditional expression evaluate only the selected operand/branch.

Writable properties and indexers support prefix and postfix ++ and --. Mutation reads through the getter, applies the increment or decrement, and writes through the setter. The receiver and each index expression are evaluated once. Prefix expressions produce the updated property value; postfix expressions produce the previous value. User-defined mutating operators on struct-valued properties are applied to the retrieved value before it is written back. For simple property and indexer assignment, the receiver is evaluated first, then the indices from left to right, then the right-hand side, each exactly once; the setter runs after those evaluations complete.

Built-in operators require compatible operand types. User-defined operators are instance methods declared on a class or struct with operator followed by the operator token. Lookup uses only the left operand's type and requires an exact parameter-type match; implicit conversions do not select an overload. Unary operators have no explicit parameter, while binary operators have one. On classes and structs, ++ and -- have no explicit parameter, return void, and mutate the receiver; prefix expressions produce the updated value and postfix expressions produce the previous value. Compound assignment operators such as += have one explicit parameter, return void, and cannot be chained. Primitive and enum extension mutation operators instead return the receiver's value type, and the compiler writes the returned value back to the operand. Equality and comparison overloads return bool. A non-generic operator member declared on a generic class or struct can be used after the type is closed over value types; its operator parameter and return types are substituted for that closed type. Operator methods may also declare method-level generic parameters inferred from the explicit operand; constraints on those parameters are checked and each closed method is emitted as a specialization. This also works on a generic class with a supported closed layout. Bodies follow the documented generic function limits. Supported tokens are +, -, *, /, %, !, ~, &, |, ^, &lt;&lt;, &gt;&gt;, ==, !=, &lt;, &lt;=, &gt;, &gt;=, ++, --, and compound assignment forms of the binary operators. CX strings implement + by concatenating their UTF-8 bytes; a null operand is treated as empty. They implement all four relational operators using ordinal UTF-8 byte ordering, which preserves Unicode scalar ordering for valid UTF-8 text. A null string sorts before a non-null string when compared through typed string values. Compound assignments to properties are supported when both a getter and setter are available. The compiler evaluates the receiver and index expressions once, reads the property, applies the compound operator, and writes the result through the setter. This includes indexed and interface-dispatched properties; named delegate properties use the same multicast combination and removal behavior as delegate variables. Function types use the syntax delegate(parameter-types) =&gt; return-type, for example delegate(int, string) =&gt; bool. Function values can be passed, stored in locals, and invoked, including directly from an indexed array access. A named static or top-level function can be used as a function value. When an expected function type is available, it selects an overload by exact parameter types and a compatible return type; generic parameters can be inferred from the expected parameter types. Lambda expressions use x =&gt; expression or (x, y) =&gt; expression, with optional block bodies. Parameter types come from the target function type or can be written explicitly, as in (int x) =&gt; x + 1. Lambdas can capture local variables, parameters, and this. Captured variables are shared by reference, so updates made by the enclosing function and by the lambda are visible to one another, even when the lambda outlives the enclosing stack frame. Capture storage is managed by the runtime garbage collector. A captured class this refers to the same object; a captured struct this is copied into managed closure storage when the closure is created. An unambiguous instance method can be used as a function value through a receiver, as in item.Read; class receivers retain the object, struct receivers are copied, and interface and virtual dispatch are preserved. An instance method can also be referenced by name inside its class instance context, including inside a lambda. An expected function type selects an instance method overload by exact parameter types and a compatible return type; generic parameters can be inferred from the expected parameter types. Static class methods can also be used as function values. Named delegate types use the declaration syntax delegate ReturnType Name(Type parameter, ...);, for example public delegate int Transform(int value);. They are nominal types, so separately declared delegate types remain distinct even when their signatures match. A lambda or function value with a compatible signature can initialize a named delegate variable. Delegate values support + and - to combine invocation lists or remove the last matching contiguous sequence, and += and -= to update a variable; compound assignment returns void. Invocation runs handlers in order, and a non-void invocation returns the last handler's result. Equality compares the ordered invocation lists, and delegates can be compared with null. GetInvocationList() is available on named delegates and anonymous function-type values. It returns a typed array with one single-cast value per entry, in invocation order; static and instance method values, including closed generic methods, use the same API. A null/default value returns an empty array. Named delegates and anonymous function types share the compiler's closure and invocation-list representation, without a common object base type. Anonymous function-type values can be initialized or assigned from null; their native value is zeroed and their invocation list is empty. DynamicInvoke(object[]) is supported for concrete reflection-supported signatures. It requires exactly one boxed argument per parameter, returns null for a null delegate or an incompatible argument list, boxes value-type results, and returns null for void. Open generic, pointer, and delegate-valued signatures are rejected; see delegate-dynamic-invoke-design.md. For mixed numeric operands, the compiler chooses a common type when one operand type accepts an implicit numeric conversion from the other; otherwise it reports an error. The current implicit numeric conversions are widening conversions among the built-in numeric types; an explicit cast is required where no such conversion applies. Reference upcasts and class-to-interface conversions are implicit. Checked downcasts and interface conversions use explicit casts and fail at runtime if the non-null value is incompatible; a null cast remains null. Type tests on null are false.

Overload resolution filters candidates by name, supplied arity, generic constraints supported by the implementation, and argument convertibility. It then selects the candidate with the better conversion for each argument. If no candidate applies, or multiple candidates remain equally good, binding reports an error; ambiguous diagnostics include candidate signatures. Literal and default parameter values and qualified enum member constants are supported on functions, methods, and constructors. Numeric defaults may have a leading + or - sign, such as int contextParameter = -1. The default literal takes its type from the parameter or another contextual target and zero-initializes that type; it is rejected where no target type is available. Omitted trailing values are inserted at each call site after overload selection. Once one parameter has a default, all following parameters must also have defaults. The compiler does not use declaration order to break ties. Generic functions, methods, classes, and interfaces may declare one class constraint followed by interface constraints, as in where T : Base, IReadable. The special constraints where T : class and where T : struct require a reference type or a non-nullable value type, respectively; either can be followed by interface constraints. Each generic parameter has one where clause. A type argument must satisfy every listed constraint at a function call or when a constructed generic type is used. Forwarding a generic parameter to a constrained type also requires compatible constraints on that parameter. Constraints may name constructed classes or interfaces. Member lookup closes those signatures against the constraint arguments, including for generic function parameters whose concrete type is a supported closed generic struct. Concept suffix constraints can also be declared on generic classes, structs, and interfaces. Their requirements are checked when a closed constructed type is resolved. In a generic class or struct member body, a single returned expression may use the constrained type parameter's required properties, methods, and operators, including built-in expressions combining those results. The body is specialized for the closed class arguments. A void member may also assign required properties and make direct required-method calls in source order. Assignment values and method-call arguments may combine literals and method parameters with required property reads and nested required method calls using built-in expressions. Required properties also support built-in +=, -=, *=, /=, and %= assignments when the right-hand side is a literal or method parameter. Other statement and control-flow forms using class-level concept requirements remain unsupported, except that a void member may group supported property assignments and required method calls in nested blocks and boolean if/else branches. Branch conditions may use the supported built-in expression forms over parameters, required members, and supported locals. A void member may declare and reassign explicitly typed built-in integer, boolean, and string locals using supported concept expressions. Integer locals also support built-in compound assignments and ++/--; boolean locals may control conditions, and string locals may be switch selectors. A local of the constrained type parameter may copy a method parameter and then use the same required methods on that local. while loop may use those expressions as its condition and contain supported property assignments or required method calls. A do/while loop has the same supported body and condition forms. A counted for loop may declare one int counter initialized from a supported expression, test it in a supported condition, and step it with prefix or postfix ++ or --; the counter may be used in supported loop-body expressions. The initializer may also assign a supported start expression to an existing int local. A bare return; may exit a class- or struct-level concept void method early. foreach (var item in values) may iterate an array whose element type is the constrained type parameter or a concrete element type such as int; its body may use the supported concept mutations and calls on the iteration variable. A switch statement may select on a supported integer, boolean, character, enum, or string concept expression and use literal or enum labels, including null and default; sections may contain the same supported mutations, calls, nested blocks, conditionals, and loops. Switch filters may use supported boolean concept expressions. make class members available in a narrow generic-function body pattern: returning a non-generic field or property value, an instance method result, or a built-in binary/conditional expression combining multiple such method calls from a parameter with a non-generic class constraint; a class-constrained function may also write multiple exposed properties or indexers in a straight-line assignment body. A supported constrained member result or expression may initialize one explicitly typed local that the function returns. Those constrained property and indexer writes also accept built-in compound assignments (+=, -=, *=, /=, and %=) when their right-hand sides use the same supported literal, parameter, binary, or conditional expressions. Assignment values may also read properties/indexers or call methods on the same constrained receiver, and combine those results with the supported built-in expressions. Compound writes evaluate receiver and indices once, read the current value, apply the built-in operator, then invoke the setter. Generic void functions may contain one or more statement-form calls to void methods on class- or interface-constrained parameters. Calls may target more than one constrained parameter. Their arguments may be literals, non-generic parameters, or supported built-in binary or conditional expressions. Calls execute in source order. Struct arguments keep the generic function's by-value parameter semantics. Constrained member-result expressions may combine calls from more than one independently constrained generic parameter, either as a direct return or as the initializer of one explicitly typed local that is returned. With a class constraint, a generic function may return a chain of ?? expressions over matching type-parameter values and null. Generic array parameters may use the same form without a constraint, as in T[] FirstNonNull&lt;T&gt;(T[] first, T[] fallback) { return first ?? fallback; }. Generic array functions may return an array's Length or compare it with an unsigned literal or parameter. Return predicates may combine multiple such comparisons with !, &&, ||, or a conditional expression, and combine them with null checks on the same array. Short-circuit operators guard the length access, as in values != null && values.Length &gt;= minimum. Method arguments may be literals, non-generic function parameters, or built-in binary/conditional expressions composed from them. A generic function may also return an instance method result exposed by a non-generic interface constraint, including a built-in binary/conditional expression combining multiple such calls, using the same argument restrictions when the inferred type argument is a reference type or a non-generic struct. Closed generic struct arguments support this method-result form and interface property reads/writes when their closed value layout and implemented interface members fit the closed-layout patterns described below. Interface-constrained property reads and indexers support direct-return bodies and built-in binary or conditional expressions composed from those reads; writes support multiple straight-line assignments for reference-type, non-generic struct, and supported closed generic struct arguments. Class- and interface-constrained assignment values may be literals, non-generic function parameters, or built-in binary/conditional expressions composed from them. Struct dispatch takes a temporary reference to the specialized value parameter. Boxed closed generic structs can dispatch through implemented non-generic interfaces. Constructed generic interfaces support T-returning direct field getters, methods returning default, and conditional generic-result getters and methods, plus void slots that assign one or more matching parameters directly to fields in source order; a matching parameter may appear at any position in a multi-parameter method. Generic interface properties whose accessors directly access a matching field are also supported. Interface methods implemented by a closed generic struct may also directly return a parameter when its substituted type matches the return type, including an enclosing generic type argument. Other generic interface member bodies remain unsupported, except non-generic methods may return default for the enclosing type parameter when called directly on a closed layout or through a constructed interface with a closed signature, and concrete-signature methods may return a built-in expression composed from concrete fields, parameters, and literals, or use a straight-line body of assignments to concrete fields with built-in expressions composed from concrete fields, parameters, and literals. These expressions are lowered against the closed struct layout in source order, and concrete-signature void methods may also use built-in +=, -=, *=, /=, and %= assignments on concrete fields when the right-hand side uses that same expression subset. Parameterless void methods may reset one or more matching generic fields to default in source order. A void method with one boolean parameter may use an if/else whose branches each reset a matching generic field to default, directly or through a constructed generic interface. Boolean if and if/else methods may assign one or more matching generic parameters to matching generic fields and reset matching generic fields to default, preserving source order. In an if without else, fields not assigned in the body remain unchanged. Branch bodies may mix these writes and resets with supported concrete-field assignments; later expressions observe earlier writes in source order. if/else branches may also use built-in compound assignments on concrete fields; later statements in a branch observe the updated values. A single-arm if may contain the same concrete-field assignments and leaves the fields unchanged when its condition is false. Concrete-signature void methods may also consist of one while loop whose condition uses concrete fields and parameters and whose body contains straight-line assignments to concrete fields, including built-in compound assignments. A single do/while loop supports the same condition and body forms, executing the body before checking its condition. One counted for loop form may assign a concrete field in its initializer, test a concrete condition, update a concrete field in its iterator, and run straight-line concrete-field assignments in its body. void methods may also mix assignments from matching generic parameters to generic fields with supported concrete expressions assigned to concrete fields, directly or through a constructed interface; both paths preserve source order. A boolean if/else may assign one or more concrete fields per branch using the same built-in concrete-expression subset; each branch's assignments preserve source order. A const getter on a concrete property may return a built-in expression over concrete fields, parameters, and literals. When it implements a property from a non-generic or constructed generic interface, its thunk evaluates the expression against the closed layout. For a constructed generic interface, the getter signature must be concrete after construction; generic-result getters support the conditional field-selection form described below. Other generic-typed computed getters remain unsupported. Concrete property setters may assign a concrete field from a built-in expression over the setter value, parameters, and literals through direct closed-layout storage or a constructed generic interface thunk with a concrete signature after construction. A generic parameter with a reference-type or class/interface type constraint, or a matching generic array parameter, may be compared with null using == or !=. Return expressions may combine such comparisons with !, &&, ||, or a conditional expression.

Statements and control flow ​

The implemented statements include blocks, local declarations and local functions, expression statements, if/else, while, do/while, for, foreach, switch, break, continue, and return. Exceptions use try, typed catch clauses, optional when filters, throw, throw; rethrow, and finally. A finally block executes when control leaves its protected region, including return, break, continue, and exception propagation. A transfer performed inside finally replaces the pending transfer. Switch statements accept integer, boolean, char, enum, and string selectors. String cases compare string contents using an ordinal, case-sensitive comparison. A case label may use when followed by a boolean filter; the filter runs only after its case value matches. Switch expressions use selector switch { label [when filter] =&gt; value, _ =&gt; fallback }. Labels are literals, enum members, or strings; string labels compare by content, and null is a valid string label. Arm values must have a compatible common type, and an unfiltered _ discard arm must appear last.

foreach iterates built-in arrays directly. String values are also iterable; each loop reads one Unicode scalar through the existing string length and index accessors. Other collections can expose a zero-argument GetEnumerator() whose result has a bool MoveNext() method and either a readable Current property or a zero-argument Current() method. The collection expression and enumerator are each evaluated once. Array&lt;T&gt;, List&lt;T&gt;, Stack&lt;T&gt;, Queue&lt;T&gt;, and LinkedList&lt;T&gt; currently use the method form; Dictionary&lt;TKey, TValue&gt; yields KeyValuePair&lt;TKey, TValue&gt; values in insertion order. Explicit iteration-variable types are resolved like local declaration types, including constructed generic types. An interface-typed IEnumerable&lt;T&gt; value can be iterated when its GetEnumerator() result implements IEnumerator&lt;T&gt;. The core generic collections expose their constructed IEnumerable&lt;T&gt; contracts, and their closed generic enumerators implement the matching IEnumerator&lt;T&gt; interface; both structural and interface-typed iteration are supported for arrays and the core collections. The core collection types implement System.Collections.ICollection&lt;T&gt;, which inherits IEnumerable&lt;T&gt; and adds a read-only uint Count property. Dictionary's collection element type is KeyValuePair&lt;TKey, TValue&gt;; built-in T[] shares Array&lt;T&gt;'s implementation.

Initialization, dispatch, and errors ​

Value fields have zero-initialized storage unless assigned by a constructor. Cross-file and cross-project access follows visibility rules, and project-reference initialization order is deterministic.

Virtual calls dispatch through class vtables. Interface values carry both a dispatch table and an instance pointer; generated interface tables support interface upcasts and method/property dispatch. Runtime type metadata supports type tests, checked casts, and read-only reflection enumeration. Reflection metadata supports dynamic construction of concrete classes that declare or inherit a public parameterless constructor, including closed generic reference classes whose supported layout is shared with their generic declaration. For non-generic and supported closed generic structs, TypeInfo.CreateInstance() returns a boxed default value with zero-initialized fields. Supported primitive, enum, and struct values can be assigned or returned as object; this creates a managed copy. An explicit cast from object restores a value only when its exact runtime type matches. Object.Type reports the boxed value type. Non-generic structs and supported closed generic structs can be boxed to implemented interfaces; generic interface support follows the limited member patterns described above. TypeInfo.CreateInstance() returns the new object, or null when the type has no supported public parameterless constructor. TypeInfo.CreateInstance(arguments) invokes a unique matching public constructor on a non-generic class or on a non-generic or supported closed generic struct. Constructor parameters may be reference types, including arrays, non-generic interfaces, or supported primitive, enum, and struct values supplied as exact-type boxes. Struct results are boxed. Unsupported or ambiguous constructor signatures return null. TypeInfo.Invoke(target, name, arguments) invokes a uniquely matching method declared on the reflected type or its base classes, preferring the nearest declaration. It supports non-generic methods with reference-type or non-generic interface parameters and a reference, interface, or void return, including supported non-virtual methods on closed generic reference classes. Interface returns are exposed as their underlying object references. Virtual methods dispatch through the target object's runtime vtable, including overrides in derived classes. Static methods are supported and ignore target. It returns null for a missing or ambiguous method, an unsupported signature, an invalid target, or incompatible arguments. A null result also represents a void return or a method that returns null. Interface return values are exposed as their underlying object references. Primitive, enum, and struct parameters and results are boxed in object values, matched by exact runtime type, and can be explicitly unboxed. Instance methods on boxed non-generic structs are supported, including mutation of the boxed payload. Closed generic struct reflection currently supports non-generic instance methods that assign matching generic parameters directly to matching fields in source order, parameterless methods returning a field value, and concrete-signature methods returning a built-in expression composed from concrete fields, parameters, and literals; parameterless void methods may reset one generic field to default, and other void methods may assign built-in expressions to concrete fields in source order. These methods mutate or read the boxed closed-layout payload. Generic methods and virtual methods declared on closed generic classes are not supported for reflection invocation.

Lexical, parse, and semantic errors include source locations where available. Syntax errors are aggregated when parser recovery can safely continue; semantic binding is fail-fast to avoid cascaded reports from invalid symbols. A failed checked cast and an uncaught exception terminate the process with diagnostics. Bounds failures and allocation failures also terminate according to the current runtime contract; they are not specified as typed CX exceptions.

Threads and synchronization ​

Import System.Threading to use the shared value handles Thread, Mutex, and AtomicInt. Copies retain the same managed state. Thread.Start accepts a delegate() =&gt; void, including a captured lambda, method value, or multicast value. Join waits for completion, publishes the worker's writes, and rethrows its failure on the joining thread; repeated joins are permitted. Normal process exit waits for owned workers and reports unobserved worker failures.

Thread.Id and static Thread.CurrentId are logical runtime IDs. Sleep(int) parks for a non-negative millisecond duration; Yield() polls and yields. Mutex.Lock/Unlock provide recursive exclusion and release/acquire publication; pair them with finally. A thread must release every mutex before exiting. AtomicInt has zero/value constructors, a synchronized Value property, Increment, Decrement, Exchange, and CompareExchange(value, comparand). Atomic adjustments wrap in the 32-bit representation. Mutable collections and application fields need explicit synchronization.

Generated functions and supported loops cooperate with stop-the-world GC. Native callers attach before managed entry, park for native-only blocking waits, and root retained managed values. Foreign callback scope/root ownership and the future task-worker contracts are specified in threading-gc-design.md.

Implementation-defined behavior and current limits ​

CX currently targets C11 runtimes on Windows (MSVC, x86/x64) and Linux (GCC, x64); macOS is not implemented. Native behavior affected by C rules, including signed integer overflow and floating-point edge cases, is not yet specified as a portable CX guarantee. String data is UTF-8; char represents a 32-bit Unicode scalar, while several Char classification helpers are ASCII-only.

The cxcore managed-memory collector is non-moving and conservative. It supports registered OS threads with cooperative safepoints; native C storage retaining managed pointers must be rooted, and dynamically unloading a module with static roots is unsupported. See the linked runtime contracts and managed-memory design for ownership, Memory.Free, and rooting rules.

Function values expose Method and Target and support DynamicInvoke for the documented concrete signatures; see delegate-reflection-design.md and delegate-dynamic-invoke-design.md. Current compiler gaps include async/await, concept features outside the operator-, method-, and property-accessor-based generic subset in concepts-design.md, and the unsupported extension target and member forms described above. Broader generic function bodies, closed layouts, and runtime-loaded generic types remain limited to the subsets described above. An associated-types direction is recorded only as a suggestion in associated-types-design.md; it has not been adopted. Concept-constrained void bodies can interleave required-property assignments, built-in compound assignments, and required method calls on one receiver, with if/else branches controlled by boolean parameters, literals, or boolean locals and !, &&, or ||. These bodies support explicitly typed locals with initializers built from literals, parameters, required property reads, and supported built-in expressions. These bodies also support while, do/while, and counted for loops with supported conditions, plus assignments to local variables and break/continue statements inside loops; other control-flow forms remain unsupported in those bodies. Bare return statements are supported for early exit; returning a value remains unsupported in these void bodies. Compound property assignments support +=, -=, *=, /=, and %= with right-hand expressions composed from literals, function parameters, required property reads, and required method calls on the same receiver. Method-call arguments may contain literals, function parameters, supported built-in expressions, and nested required method calls or property reads on that receiver. The target property is read before the right-hand expression and written afterward; overloaded operators and indexers are not supported by this concept-body form. Foreach loops over arrays with concrete element types or nested arrays of the constrained type parameter are also supported. Required method signatures may use the constrained self type inside an array parameter, with the concrete type substituted during specialization. Integer, character, boolean, and enum parameters can also be selected with a switch statement containing literal labels and mutation statements. The grammar accepts an async modifier, but it has no async semantics; await is not implemented. Generic support is restricted to the body and layout patterns in generics-design.md, including selecting between matching generic values with a conditional expression, returning an indexed element from a matching generic array parameter directly or through an explicitly typed or inferred matching generic local followed by matching local copies or reassignments, or returning the element from Get(uint) on a matching T[] or Array&lt;T&gt; parameter, reading its length, and comparing a matching generic array's length with a non-negative integer literal (with or without a u suffix) or uint parameter, or comparing the lengths of two matching generic arrays using T[] and Array&lt;T&gt; spellings, including nested array access. A length may also be compared with an unsigned arithmetic expression over uint parameters and non-negative integer literals using +, -, *, /, or %; assigning a matching value to one indexed element or copying one indexed element between matching generic array parameters, constructing and filling a matching generic array, comparing a reference-constrained generic value or matching generic array with null, and copying a matching generic array with the documented indexed for or while loop, or a foreach over the source array. A generic void function or non-static method may also forward one call to another generic void function or method when at least one direct argument carries a caller type parameter; exact specializations and primary fallback are selected for each closed caller type. Jagged array types preserve all array ranks, and allocation supports trailing unsized ranks such as new int[1][]. Generic functions may return, assign, or copy nested array elements, read a nested array's length, or compare it with a non-negative integer literal (with or without a u suffix) or a uint operand; generic property accessors and using closed generic properties in expressions are supported for the documented field-backed patterns, including nested constructed class-reference types. Closed generic layouts may also contain concrete primitive, reference, enum, or array fields, and non-generic or closed constructed generic structs stored by value. Closed generic reference layouts also support concrete primitive, array, and non-generic struct fields, including matching constructor parameter assignments and direct-field properties. They may also store a constructed interface field such as IEqualityComparer&lt;TKey&gt; and initialize it from a matching constructor parameter; mixed constructors may initialize concrete array fields with uint literals or supported built-in expressions over constructor parameters and literals. These interface fields keep the existing cx_iface_ref representation. They may derive from one generic or non-generic base class when the base hierarchy uses only inherited System.Object virtual slots and no interfaces. Each closed class in that hierarchy must satisfy the shared-reference-layout constraints, and forwarded type arguments must satisfy each base class's generic constraints. Closed generic layouts are emitted in dependency order. Constructed generic struct fields support empty parameterless constructors and constructor assignments from a matching constructed generic struct parameter; their type arguments may depend on the enclosing type parameter. In a supported closed generic struct constructor, one matching parameter may initialize multiple fields; fields not assigned by the constructor retain their zero-initialized or expression-initialized values. Concrete fields in closed generic layouts may have initializers composed of literals and built-in unary or binary operators; these run before constructor assignments. Null initializers are supported for array fields and T fields with reference-type or class constraints. A direct T field in a supported closed generic layout may also use the default initializer. Constructed generic fields may also use default, for example Box&lt;T&gt; Value = default; or Pair&lt;T&gt; Value = default;. Concrete properties on closed generic structs may use const getters that return built-in expressions over concrete fields, parameters, and literals. The expression is evaluated against the closed layout, including for supported interface dispatch. A concrete property setter may assign a concrete field from a built-in expression over its value, parameters, and literals when written through direct closed-layout storage or through a constructed generic interface thunk when its signature is concrete after construction. A const T getter may conditionally return a matching T field or default, or select between two matching T fields, based on a concrete boolean-field expression, when read directly from a closed generic struct. This generic-result form also supports constructed generic interface thunks when the constructed result type is supported. A generic-typed getter may also initialize one explicitly typed or inferred local from a matching field (written directly or as this.field), or select a matching field or default using boolean fields, literals, !, &&, or ||, and return that local; this lowers to the same field read or conditional selection as a direct getter, including through a constructed-interface thunk. Other generic-typed computed getters and broader accessor bodies remain unsupported. Closed generic structs may also return this conditional generic-result form from a method with concrete parameters, called directly or through a constructed generic interface; both paths evaluate against the closed layout. Such a method may express the selection either as a conditional expression or as an if/else whose branches each return one matching generic field or default. It may also be called through a generic function constrained by that constructed interface type. Methods with concrete return types may use the same if/else shape when each branch returns a supported built-in expression over concrete fields, parameters, and literals; direct calls, constructed-interface thunks, and interface-constrained generic calls are supported. Method calls, variable references other than the earlier concrete fields described below, overloaded operators, and other generic-typed field initializers remain unsupported. A closed generic reference class may initialize a concrete non-generic class field with a parameterless new expression, or a concrete field with a constructed generic class or struct new expression whose arguments are literals or supported built-in expressions over earlier concrete fields. A constructed target may use the owner's type parameters; the target and constructor close separately for each closed owner. Reference and value initializers run before the owner constructor body; see generic-constructed-field-initializer-design.md. Closed generic reference classes may also initialize an array field whose element is a constructed generic class or struct type such as Box&lt;T&gt;[] or Pair&lt;T&gt;[]; the element type arguments close separately for each owner, and struct elements require a supported closed value layout. A constructor may allocate the same array shape using a supported uint length expression over its parameters and literals. Non-generic static fields may also allocate arrays in the module initializer; see static-array-field-initializers-design.md and generic-array-field-initializer-design.md. An explicit constructor in a closed generic struct may also initialize an array field whose element type is concrete, the owner type parameter, or a supported constructed generic type. The allocation uses the closed element size; default struct values remain zero-initialized. See generic-struct-array-initializers-design.md. Closed generic field initializers may also read earlier concrete instance fields in declaration order; self, forward, static, and generic-field references are outside that subset. See generic-field-initializer-order-design.md. An initializer may call a non-generic instance method through an earlier concrete reference field when the method signature and arguments are concrete; the earlier field is initialized before the call. Calls through other receiver forms are outside this subset. The same design note describes this boundary. They may also allocate concrete array fields, or T[] fields where T is an owner type parameter, with a uint literal length or a supported built-in expression over earlier concrete fields and literals; each owner gets its own storage with the closed element size. See generic-array-field-initializer-design.md. Broader accessor bodies and layouts remain limited. Instance field initializers may use expressions and are evaluated in the constructor after base initialization. Static field initializers may use expressions; dynamic values are assigned during module initialization after referenced modules initialize and before the executable entry point. Within a module, initializers follow the deterministic generated type order and each type's field declaration order. Consult compiler diagnostics and tests for the exact supported subset of each feature.

Native C interoperability and UTF-16 ​

@Name annotations use exact type names and positional/named constant constructor arguments. Named annotation arguments use name = value; ordinary calls retain name: value. User annotations derive from System.Annotation; AnnotationUsage defines targets and repeatability. @return:Tag targets a function result. Annotations are compile-time metadata; compilation never executes constructors.

System.Interop.NativeImport selects a foreign C symbol on a nongeneric extern top-level function/static method. Plain extern retains the CX ABI. Native signatures use scalars, typed pointers, checked native records and native function pointers; managed values are not automatically marshaled. Raw calls require an unsafe function or unsafe { ... } block. SDK declarations validate signatures and layout.

cx
import System.Interop;
@NativeImport("kernel32", entryPoint = "GetTickCount",
    callingConvention = NativeCallingConvention.Winapi)
public extern uint TickCount();
public uint Elapsed() { unsafe { return TickCount(); } }
1
2
3
4
5

Declare the logical library in native_libraries in the project. Target CMake selects OS, architecture and compiler settings. Supported ABIs are MSVC Windows x86/x64 and GCC/Clang Linux x64. Cdecl, Stdcall, Winapi and PlatformDefault are explicit; SDK-backed PlatformDefault honors the SDK convention. Optional errno and Windows last-error capture happens immediately after the call.

ptr&lt;T&gt; preserves the pointee; ptr&lt;const T&gt; differs from const ptr&lt;T&gt;. Null, address-of native locals, dereference/indexing, pointer-to-pointer parameters and explicit conversions require unsafe operations. ptr&lt;const void&gt; is a read-only void borrow. CLong/CULong, SizeT, PtrDiffT and IntPtr/UIntPtr map to target C scalars; CX long remains 64-bit. NativeType uses SDK records/scalars/opaque types; opaque types are legal through pointers only. NativeLayout supports sequential and union storage, packing, alignment, checked offsets and inline T[count] fields. Native enums have explicit underlying types. sizeof/alignof/offsetof query native storage; stackalloc<T>(count) allocates aligned caller storage, limited to 1 MiB. Known stack borrows cannot escape or enter a parked blocking native call.

wchar is an unsigned 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, distinct from scalar char and C wchar_t. Out-of-range constant conversions are diagnosed. WideString is immutable: Length/Item use code units, ScalarCount/ScalarAt use validated scalars. Embedded zeros are preserved. String.ToWideString and WideString.ToString explicitly and strictly transcode; ToString overrides Object.ToString. EncodingException.Position reports the failing byte/unit. No implicit conversion or automatic native marshaling exists. NativeBuffer makes owned UTF-8/UTF-16 copies and length-based output strings; Dispose is explicit. AllocateAligned supports records with stronger alignment.

NativeFunction delegates contain a single typed native function pointer. Static noncapturing CX functions convert to guarded callback entries. Captured callbacks use NativeCallback.Register<T> with an explicit native context parameter and rooted registration. Unregister runs SDK cleanup and waits for in-flight callbacks. Exceptions produce an ABI-valid failure result and are available through callback failure APIs. Foreign threads attach to the GC; blocking imports support reentry. NativeLibrary.Load/Resolve<T> provide explicit runtime discovery, with libraries kept open until process exit. Symbol-only function values differ from data pointers.

The complete ownership, dependency and callback contract is in ../../cxcore/docs/native-interop-design.md; SDK binding examples are in ../../examples/native-bindings. C varargs, C++/COM, automatic marshaling/header generation, unloading and runtime annotation reflection remain later features.
